title: HTTP caching from the browser to the CDN to React Query
description: Follow one request outward through every cache it can hit: the browser's HTTP cache (`Cache-Control`, `ETag`, `Last-Modified`, revalidation), the CDN edge, the client query cache (React Query and SWR), and the server's own cache. Then tackle the hard part, invalidation. You'll meet strong and weak validators, `stale-while-revalidate`, cache stampedes, request coalescing, negative caching, and cache keys. Each explanation links to the RFC or docs behind the answer.

questions.title: Who coined the "two hard things in Computer Science" quip?
questions.description: Complete the attribution: *"There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things."*

options.text: Phil Karlton
Donald Knuth
Leslie Lamport
Martin Fowler

questions.explanation: The line comes from **Phil Karlton**, an engineer at Netscape. Cache invalidation means deciding when a stored copy no longer matches the truth, and that question runs through this whole quiz. Knuth is known for "premature optimization is the root of all evil", and Lamport for his work on distributed systems. Fowler made the quote popular on his blog, but he credits Karlton.

questions.title: What does `Cache-Control: no-cache` actually permit?
questions.description: A response carries `Cache-Control: no-cache`.

options.text: The cache may store the response, but must revalidate with the origin before reusing it
The cache must not store the response anywhere
The response may be reused freely for the rest of the session
Only the browser cache is forbidden; shared caches may reuse it

questions.explanation: The name is misleading. `no-cache` lets the cache store the response, but the cache has to check with the origin before each reuse. On the next request it sends a conditional request (`If-None-Match` or `If-Modified-Since`). If the origin answers `304 Not Modified`, the cache serves its stored body without downloading it again. So `no-cache` with an `ETag` is cheap. You still make the round trip, but you skip the body. The directive that forbids storage is `no-store`, which the next question covers.

questions.title: When does `no-store` belong on a response?

options.text: A bank statement page that no cache should ever write to disk or memory
A logo that changes once a year and should be cached for a long time
An API response that should be reused but checked for freshness each time
A fingerprinted JS bundle that will never change under its URL

questions.explanation: `no-store` is the strictest directive. No cache may store any part of the request or response, whether it's the browser's disk cache or a proxy in between. Use it for sensitive content that nobody should reuse, like statements or one-time tokens. The other options all want caching. The logo wants a long `max-age`, the API response wants `no-cache` (store it, but revalidate every time), and the fingerprinted bundle wants `max-age=31536000, immutable`. Putting `no-store` on cacheable content costs performance, and nothing warns you about it.

questions.title: What does `Cache-Control: private` tell caches?

images.alt: A GET descends three rows: the private browser cache, the shared CDN edge, then the origin. A fresh browser copy is served with no network at all. Past max-age=60 the request reaches the edge, which is still fresh under s-maxage=600 and returns the body with Age: 200. Past 600 seconds the edge revalidates with If-None-Match: "v7"; a matching ETag yields 304 with no body, a differing one yields 200 with a new body and validator.
images.caption: The left column is the private row. The middle column is the shared one.

options.text: Only a single-user (browser) cache may store it; shared caches must not
The response is encrypted and must be served over HTTPS
No cache of any kind may store the response
It may only be stored by shared caches, not the browser

questions.explanation: `private` controls who may store a response. It has nothing to do with encryption. It marks the response as meant for one user, so a shared cache (a CDN or proxy) must not keep it, while the user's own browser cache may. `public` works the other way. It lets a shared cache store a response it would otherwise skip, such as one to a request with an `Authorization` header. If you read `private` as "secret" or "encrypted", you'll fall for the distractors. It only says which caches may store the response and gives no confidentiality.

questions.title: Why is the CDN serving one user's data to everyone, and what's the fix?
questions.description:
An app serves each logged-in user's dashboard through a CDN. Users start seeing *other people's* names. The origin sends:

```http
Cache-Control: max-age=60
```

images.alt: A GET descends three rows: the private browser cache, the shared CDN edge, then the origin. A fresh browser copy is served with no network at all. Past max-age=60 the request reaches the edge, which is still fresh under s-maxage=600 and returns the body with Age: 200. Past 600 seconds the edge revalidates with If-None-Match: "v7"; a matching ETag yields 304 with no body, a differing one yields 200 with a new body and validator.
images.caption: Without `private`, the shared middle row stores the response and serves it to the next visitor.

options.text: Without `private`, the shared CDN may cache the response; per-user responses need `Cache-Control: private, no-store` (or `private`)
`max-age` is too high; lowering it to `10` fixes the leak
The CDN needs `Vary: Accept-Encoding` added
The browser cache is leaking; add `no-cache`

questions.explanation: A plain `max-age=60` without `private` lets shared caches store the response. The CDN caches the first user's dashboard under the URL and serves it to every visitor for the next 60 seconds. That's a data leak between users. `private` fixes it by keeping the response out of the shared cache, and `no-store` is safer still for sensitive pages. A lower `max-age` only shortens the leak. `Vary: Accept-Encoding` separates compressed variants, not users. And the browser cache belongs to one user, so it was never the problem.

questions.title: How long does each cache treat this response as fresh?
questions.description: A response is sent with `Cache-Control: max-age=60, s-maxage=600`.

images.alt: A GET descends three rows: the private browser cache, the shared CDN edge, then the origin. A fresh browser copy is served with no network at all. Past max-age=60 the request reaches the edge, which is still fresh under s-maxage=600 and returns the body with Age: 200. Past 600 seconds the edge revalidates with If-None-Match: "v7"; a matching ETag yields 304 with no body, a differing one yields 200 with a new body and validator.
images.caption: One response with two deadlines, 60 s for the browser row and 600 s for the edge row.

options.text: Browser cache: 60s; shared cache (CDN/proxy): 600s
Both caches: 60s, since `s-maxage` is only a hint
Both caches: 600s, since the larger value always wins
Browser cache: 600s; shared cache: 60s

questions.explanation: `s-maxage` overrides `max-age` **for shared caches only**. The browser ignores it. So the browser keeps its copy fresh for 60 seconds, and the CDN keeps its copy for 600. This split is the usual setup for edge caching. The short browser lifetime lets users see updates quickly, and the longer edge lifetime keeps traffic off the origin. (`s-maxage` also implies `proxy-revalidate`.) The two numbers are meant for different caches, which is why neither "only a hint" nor "the larger value wins" is right.

questions.title: Which HTTP status code lets the cache reuse its copy *without* receiving the body again?
questions.description: A cache sends `If-None-Match` with the stored `ETag`. The representation hasn't changed.

images.alt: A GET descends three rows: the private browser cache, the shared CDN edge, then the origin. A fresh browser copy is served with no network at all. Past max-age=60 the request reaches the edge, which is still fresh under s-maxage=600 and returns the body with Age: 200. Past 600 seconds the edge revalidates with If-None-Match: "v7"; a matching ETag yields 304 with no body, a differing one yields 200 with a new body and validator.
images.caption: The bottom-left branch. The validator still matches, so no body crosses the wire.

questions.explanation: `304 Not Modified` is what validators are for. The origin sends a small response with headers only, confirming that the cached copy is still good, and the cache serves the body it already has. That's why `no-cache` and `max-age=0, must-revalidate` are cheap when paired with an `ETag` or `Last-Modified`. You pay for one round trip but skip the payload. `200 OK` would send the full body again. `412 Precondition Failed` belongs to write preconditions like `If-Match`, not to revalidating a GET.

questions.title: Which rule does a correct `304 Not Modified` response follow?

images.alt: A GET descends three rows: the private browser cache, the shared CDN edge, then the origin. A fresh browser copy is served with no network at all. Past max-age=60 the request reaches the edge, which is still fresh under s-maxage=600 and returns the body with Age: 200. Past 600 seconds the edge revalidates with If-None-Match: "v7"; a matching ETag yields 304 with no body, a differing one yields 200 with a new body and validator.
images.caption: The 304 branch carries only headers. The stored copy supplies the body.

options.text: It must not include a message body; the cache reuses the stored representation
It must repeat the full body so the cache can verify the bytes
It must drop the `ETag` header to signal the match
It must include `Content-Length: 0` and an empty body block

questions.explanation: A `304` has no body on purpose, because sending the payload again would defeat revalidation. The origin returns the status and updated headers. It *should* keep the `ETag`, and it may refresh `Cache-Control`, `Date`, and similar headers. The cache then serves the body it already stored. Sending a body or removing the `ETag` would break the mechanism. `204 No Content` also has no body, but it means "the request succeeded and there's nothing to return", not "your cached copy is still valid".

questions.title: When a cache revalidates a stored GET response, which headers carry which validator?

images.alt: A GET descends three rows: the private browser cache, the shared CDN edge, then the origin. A fresh browser copy is served with no network at all. Past max-age=60 the request reaches the edge, which is still fresh under s-maxage=600 and returns the body with Age: 200. Past 600 seconds the edge revalidates with If-None-Match: "v7"; a matching ETag yields 304 with no body, a differing one yields 200 with a new body and validator.
images.caption: The stored `ETag` goes back out as `If-None-Match` on the revalidation arrow.

options.text: `If-None-Match` carries the `ETag`; `If-Modified-Since` carries the `Last-Modified` date
`If-Match` carries the `ETag`; `If-Unmodified-Since` carries the `Last-Modified` date
`If-None-Match` carries the `Last-Modified` date; `If-Modified-Since` carries the `ETag`
The client sends `ETag`; the server replies with `If-Modified-Since`

questions.explanation: The cache sends back the validators it stored. The `ETag` goes in `If-None-Match`, and the `Last-Modified` date goes in `If-Modified-Since`. If they match, the origin replies `304`. `If-Match` and `If-Unmodified-Since` look similar but do the opposite job. They guard *writes* ("only PUT if nothing changed"), and a mismatch returns `412`. Also, the server sends validators first, because `ETag` and `Last-Modified` are response headers. The client only sends the `If-*` versions.

questions.title: What does the `W/` prefix on an ETag mean?
questions.description:
An origin sends:

```http
ETag: W/"7e3a91"
```

options.text: A weak validator: the representations mean the same thing but may differ byte for byte
The ETag is a wildcard that matches any request
The response was served over a WebSocket
The ETag is weakly encrypted and should be treated as untrusted

questions.explanation: `W/` marks a **weak** ETag. Two representations with the same weak ETag mean the same thing, but their bytes may differ. That helps when small differences shouldn't invalidate the cache, like the same page with and without gzip, or with a regenerated timestamp comment. A **strong** ETag (no prefix) promises identical bytes. The prefix isn't a wildcard (the wildcard is `*`, as in `If-None-Match: *`), and it says nothing about transport or encryption.

questions.title: Why does a range request need a **strong** ETag, not a weak one?
questions.description: A client resumes a partial download with `Range` and `If-Range`.

options.text: Joining new bytes to bytes the client already has needs identical bytes, and only a strong validator guarantees that
Weak ETags expire faster than strong ones
Range requests are not allowed to use `ETag` at all, only `Last-Modified`
Weak ETags are too short to encode a byte offset

questions.explanation: A range request joins a newly fetched byte range to bytes the client already holds. If the representation changed by even one byte, the result is corrupt. So the comparison needs a **strong** validator, which promises identical bytes. A weak ETag only promises the same meaning, which isn't enough to join bytes safely, and the spec forbids weak validators here. ETag length doesn't matter, and `If-Range` accepts an `ETag` as long as it's strong.

questions.title: Why can `Last-Modified` alone (with no `ETag`) serve an outdated body even though revalidation "succeeded"?

options.text: HTTP dates have one-second resolution, so two edits within the same second look identical
`Last-Modified` is always in the client's local time zone
Browsers ignore `Last-Modified` unless `ETag` is also present
`Last-Modified` only works for images, not HTML or JSON

questions.explanation: HTTP dates count whole seconds, so their resolution is exactly **1 second**. If a file changes twice in the same second, the timestamp stays the same, and `If-Modified-Since` returns `304` for content that did change. The cache then serves an outdated copy. An `ETag` avoids this because you can derive it from a content hash or a version counter that changes on every edit. (HTTP dates are always in GMT, and `Last-Modified` works for any content type.) For resources that change often, prefer strong ETags.

questions.title: Which directive lets a cache return a stale response *immediately* while it revalidates in the background?
questions.description: It's a `Cache-Control` extension directive from RFC 5861. Type the token exactly as it appears in the header.

images.alt: A timeline of one stored response sent with max-age=600 and stale-while-revalidate=86400: a green FRESH band up to 600 seconds, an orange stale-but-inside-the-window band up to 87,000 seconds, then a dashed EXPIRED band that requires a round trip. A marker at 700 seconds falls inside the orange band. Below, four cards state what stale-while-revalidate, stale-if-error, must-revalidate and immutable each change at the boundary, and a final note gives the 10-percent-of-Date-minus-Last-Modified heuristic for a response with no freshness headers.
images.caption: The orange band is the `stale-while-revalidate` window.

questions.explanation: With `stale-while-revalidate=<seconds>`, a response can go stale without making anyone wait. For up to N seconds after it goes stale, the cache may serve the old copy at once and refresh it in the background, so the *next* request gets fresh data. The client-side "SWR" pattern and the SWR React library take their name from this directive. Its sibling, `stale-if-error`, handles a different case, serving stale content when the origin is *down*.

questions.title: What does the user get **700 seconds** after the response was stored?
questions.description: A response carries `Cache-Control: max-age=600, stale-while-revalidate=86400`.

images.alt: A timeline of one stored response sent with max-age=600 and stale-while-revalidate=86400: a green FRESH band up to 600 seconds, an orange stale-but-inside-the-window band up to 87,000 seconds, then a dashed EXPIRED band that requires a round trip. A marker at 700 seconds falls inside the orange band. Below, four cards state what stale-while-revalidate, stale-if-error, must-revalidate and immutable each change at the boundary, and a final note gives the 10-percent-of-Date-minus-Last-Modified heuristic for a response with no freshness headers.
images.caption: The 700 s marker sits inside the orange band, not past it.

options.text: The stale copy comes back immediately, and the cache revalidates in the background for next time
The request blocks until the origin returns a fresh copy
The cache returns a `504` because the entry is past `max-age`
The stale copy is discarded and a `200` with no body is returned

questions.explanation: At 700 seconds the entry is stale (past `max-age=600`) but well inside the `stale-while-revalidate=86400` window. The cache serves the stale body **with no extra delay** and fetches a fresh copy in the background for later requests. The user gets a fast answer that may be slightly out of date, which suits dashboards and feeds. SWR exists to avoid blocking on the origin. A `504` could only appear once the window has passed, the origin can't be reached, and no directive allows serving stale content.

questions.title: Which directive lets a cache keep serving a stale copy when revalidation *fails* (the origin errors or can't be reached)?

images.alt: A timeline of one stored response sent with max-age=600 and stale-while-revalidate=86400: a green FRESH band up to 600 seconds, an orange stale-but-inside-the-window band up to 87,000 seconds, then a dashed EXPIRED band that requires a round trip. A marker at 700 seconds falls inside the orange band. Below, four cards state what stale-while-revalidate, stale-if-error, must-revalidate and immutable each change at the boundary, and a final note gives the 10-percent-of-Date-minus-Last-Modified heuristic for a response with no freshness headers.
images.caption: `stale-if-error` is the orange band's counterpart for when the origin fails.

options.text: `stale-if-error`
`must-revalidate`
`no-cache`
`immutable`

questions.explanation: `stale-if-error=<seconds>` keeps a site up when the origin has problems. Within its window, if revalidation gets a `5xx` or a connection failure, the cache may serve the last good response instead of showing the error. `must-revalidate` does nearly the opposite. It forbids serving a stale copy after expiry, and the cache returns `504` if it can't reach the origin. `no-cache` requires revalidation before every reuse, and `immutable` skips revalidation while the entry is fresh.

questions.title: What does adding `must-revalidate` to `max-age=60` change in practice?

images.alt: A timeline of one stored response sent with max-age=600 and stale-while-revalidate=86400: a green FRESH band up to 600 seconds, an orange stale-but-inside-the-window band up to 87,000 seconds, then a dashed EXPIRED band that requires a round trip. A marker at 700 seconds falls inside the orange band. Below, four cards state what stale-while-revalidate, stale-if-error, must-revalidate and immutable each change at the boundary, and a final note gives the 10-percent-of-Date-minus-Last-Modified heuristic for a response with no freshness headers.
images.caption: `must-revalidate` removes the orange band, so nothing stale is ever served.

options.text: Once the entry is stale, the cache may not serve it without successful revalidation, even if the origin is unreachable
It forces revalidation on every request, even while the entry is still fresh
It doubles the freshness lifetime to 120 seconds
It allows shared caches to ignore `max-age`

questions.explanation: By default, a cache may sometimes serve stale content, for example when it's offline. `must-revalidate` takes that option away. After `max-age` runs out, the cache can use the stored copy only if revalidation succeeds. If it can't reach the origin, it must return `504 Gateway Timeout` instead. It does **not** force revalidation while the entry is still fresh (`no-cache` and `max-age=0` do that), and it doesn't change any lifetimes. Use it when stale data would cause real harm, such as prices.

questions.title: What does `immutable` add beyond a year-long `max-age`?
questions.description: A fingerprinted asset is served with `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable`.

images.alt: A timeline of one stored response sent with max-age=600 and stale-while-revalidate=86400: a green FRESH band up to 600 seconds, an orange stale-but-inside-the-window band up to 87,000 seconds, then a dashed EXPIRED band that requires a round trip. A marker at 700 seconds falls inside the orange band. Below, four cards state what stale-while-revalidate, stale-if-error, must-revalidate and immutable each change at the boundary, and a final note gives the 10-percent-of-Date-minus-Last-Modified heuristic for a response with no freshness headers.
images.caption: `immutable` acts inside the green band, when the user reloads.

options.text: It stops the conditional request the browser would otherwise send when the user reloads while the entry is fresh
It makes the asset un-deletable from the cache until `max-age` expires
It encrypts the asset so intermediaries can't read it
It forces the browser to download a fresh copy on every reload

questions.explanation: When a user hits *Reload*, browsers usually send a conditional request to check freshness. For an asset with a hashed URL like `app.7e3a91.js`, that round trip is wasted, because the content under that URL can never change. `immutable` tells the browser not to revalidate while the entry is fresh, so those reload-time `304`s go away. It doesn't protect the entry from eviction, encrypt anything, or force downloads. With it, repeat loads of content-hashed bundles cost no requests at all.

questions.title: For how many hours will a cache treat this response as fresh?
questions.description: A response has **no** `Cache-Control` and **no** `Expires`, only a `Last-Modified`. The origin generated it (its `Date`) exactly **200 hours** after the resource was last modified. Use the common 10% heuristic that RFC 9111 suggests, and enter a number.

images.alt: A timeline of one stored response sent with max-age=600 and stale-while-revalidate=86400: a green FRESH band up to 600 seconds, an orange stale-but-inside-the-window band up to 87,000 seconds, then a dashed EXPIRED band that requires a round trip. A marker at 700 seconds falls inside the orange band. Below, four cards state what stale-while-revalidate, stale-if-error, must-revalidate and immutable each change at the boundary, and a final note gives the 10-percent-of-Date-minus-Last-Modified heuristic for a response with no freshness headers.
images.caption: The blue note gives the formula, 10% of `Date` − `Last-Modified`.

questions.explanation: Without explicit freshness headers, a cache *may* guess a lifetime. RFC 9111 suggests using at most a fraction of the time since `Last-Modified`, and **10%** is the usual choice (Apache `httpd` has used it as a default for years). Here `Date − Last-Modified = 200 h`, so `0.10 × 200 = 20 hours`. Leaving out caching headers doesn't stop caching. It lets the cache guess, and the guess can keep content much longer than you expect. Always set freshness explicitly.

questions.title: What does `Vary: Accept-Encoding` tell caches to do?

options.text: Store a separate copy for each request `Accept-Encoding` value, so gzip and uncompressed clients each get the right body
Refresh the response whenever the `Accept-Encoding` header changes server-side
Compress the response with whatever encoding the client prefers
Forbid caching unless the client sends `Accept-Encoding`

questions.explanation: `Vary` adds request headers to the cache key, which is otherwise just the URL. With `Vary: Accept-Encoding`, one URL can have several stored copies, say one gzipped and one uncompressed, and the cache picks the one that matches the request's `Accept-Encoding`. Without it, a cache could send a gzipped body to a client that can't decode it. `Vary` only affects the cache key. It doesn't compress anything or trigger a refresh. The origin still does the encoding, and `Vary` keeps the copies apart.

questions.title: What will probably happen if you add `Vary: User-Agent` to shared, cacheable HTML?

options.text: The hit rate collapses, because there are so many different UA strings that the cache splits into countless copies
Caching speeds up, since each browser gets a dedicated fast path
Nothing changes; `User-Agent` is not a valid `Vary` value
The origin stops receiving any traffic at all

questions.explanation: Each distinct `User-Agent` string becomes its own cache key. UA strings differ by browser, version, OS, and device, so the shared cache fills with copies that each get requested once or twice. Most requests miss and go to the origin, which defeats the point of the cache. Only `Vary` on headers with a few possible values that you actually branch on, like `Accept-Encoding`. If you need to adapt to the device type, reduce it to a few values first, for example with an edge-computed `Vary: X-Device-Type`, instead of varying on the raw `User-Agent`.

questions.title: What does `Age: 550` tell you?
questions.description: A response comes back from a CDN with `Cache-Control: max-age=600` and `Age: 550`.

images.alt: A GET descends three rows: the private browser cache, the shared CDN edge, then the origin. A fresh browser copy is served with no network at all. Past max-age=60 the request reaches the edge, which is still fresh under s-maxage=600 and returns the body with Age: 200. Past 600 seconds the edge revalidates with If-None-Match: "v7"; a matching ETag yields 304 with no body, a differing one yields 200 with a new body and validator.
images.caption: In the diagram, `Age: 200` against `s-maxage=600` leaves 400 s of edge freshness.

options.text: The copy has been in caches for about 550 seconds, so it stays fresh for only about 50 more
The response will be deleted from the cache in 550 seconds
The origin server has been running for 550 seconds
The client must wait 550 seconds before using the response

questions.explanation: `Age` is a shared cache's estimate of how many seconds have passed since the origin generated or last validated the response. With `max-age=600` and `Age: 550`, the copy stays fresh for `600 − 550 = 50` more seconds. After that it's stale and needs revalidation, unless `stale-while-revalidate` allows serving it. When `Age` is close to `max-age`, you're getting an old copy from the edge. Check it when you're debugging why you still see old content.

questions.title: Which responses should a shared CDN cache refuse to store by default?
questions.description: Several responses arrive at a shared CDN cache. Select **every** one that applies.

options.text: `Cache-Control: private, max-age=600`
`Cache-Control: no-store`
A 200 response to a request that carried an `Authorization` header, with no `public`, `s-maxage`, or `must-revalidate`
`Cache-Control: public, max-age=600`

questions.explanation: A shared cache must refuse three of these. `private` rules out shared caches. `no-store` rules out every cache. And by default a shared cache must not store a response to a request with an `Authorization` header, unless `public`, `s-maxage`, or `must-revalidate` allows it. That rule stops one user's authenticated content from reaching other users. Only `public, max-age=600` is free for the CDN to store. The `Authorization` rule is the easy one to miss, and it explains many cases of "why is my logged-in API response cached at the edge?"

questions.title: What is the "stampede" that follows a hot key's expiry?
questions.description: A very popular key expires in a Redis-backed cache. The problem is also called *thundering herd* or *dog-piling*.

images.alt: Two panels. Without coalescing, five GET boxes standing in for 5,000 concurrent misses all arrow into one origin box marked 5,000 identical recomputations. With coalescing, the same requests arrow into a single-flight gate labelled one leader, 4,999 waiters, and a single arrow continues to an origin box marked 1 recomputation. Below, four cards name request coalescing, serving stale while revalidating, probabilistic early expiration and TTL jitter, and a final card marks max-age=0 as the opposite of a fix.
images.caption: In the left panel, every concurrent miss recomputes the same value.

options.text: Many concurrent requests miss at once and all hit the origin to recompute the same value
The cache evicts every other key to make room for the recomputed one
The CDN floods the cache with duplicate copies of the response
Clients retry so fast that the browser cache overflows to disk

questions.explanation: A stampede starts the moment a hot key expires. The cached value is gone, every request in flight misses at the same time, and they all ask the origin (a database or upstream API) to rebuild the **same** value. All that duplicate work can overload the backend and cause slowdowns or an outage, right when traffic peaks. The fixes combine those concurrent requests into one, as the next question shows. Eviction and duplicate storage, which the distractors describe, aren't the problem.

questions.title: Which techniques actually prevent a cache stampede on a hot key?
questions.description: Select **every** technique that applies.

images.alt: Two panels. Without coalescing, five GET boxes standing in for 5,000 concurrent misses all arrow into one origin box marked 5,000 identical recomputations. With coalescing, the same requests arrow into a single-flight gate labelled one leader, 4,999 waiters, and a single arrow continues to an origin box marked 1 recomputation. Below, four cards name request coalescing, serving stale while revalidating, probabilistic early expiration and TTL jitter, and a final card marks max-age=0 as the opposite of a fix.
images.caption: Four techniques that each stop N requests from doing the same work N times.

options.text: Request coalescing (single-flight): combine concurrent identical misses into one origin fetch and share the result
Serve the stale value while a single worker revalidates in the background
Probabilistic early expiration: refresh a hot key shortly *before* it expires, so one request recomputes instead of all of them
Add random jitter to TTLs so many keys don't expire at the same instant
Set `max-age=0` so every request always recomputes at the origin

questions.explanation: All four real fixes stop N requests from doing the same work N times. With **single-flight**, one request fetches and the rest wait for its result. **Serving stale while revalidating** keeps answering from the old value, so only one refresh runs. With **probabilistic early expiration** (the XFetch approach), one request refreshes the key before it expires, so the key never goes cold under heavy traffic. **TTL jitter** spreads out expiry times so caches don't all miss together. `max-age=0` does the opposite. It sends every request to the origin, which is a stampede that never ends.
questions.references: [Vattani, Chierichetti & Lowenstein: *Optimal Probabilistic Cache Stampede Prevention* (VLDB 2015)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol8/p886-vattani.pdf)

questions.title: What is this `404`-caching technique called, and what is its main risk?
questions.description: A lookup service caches `404 Not Found` results for a short time.

options.text: Negative caching: it spares the backend repeated lookups of missing keys, but can briefly hide a resource that was just created
Write-through caching: every miss is written back to the database
Cache poisoning: an attacker injects a fake 404 into the cache
Eviction: 404s are stored to decide which keys to drop first

questions.explanation: **Negative caching** stores the result that something doesn't exist, such as a `404`, an empty lookup, or a DNS `NXDOMAIN`. Then a flood of requests for a missing key doesn't keep hitting the backend. DNS makes this official in RFC 2308, which caches negative answers for the SOA `MINIMUM` TTL. The risk is the reverse kind of staleness. If someone creates the resource moments later, clients keep getting the cached "not found" until the entry expires, so keep negative TTLs short. The other options are unrelated: write-through is a write policy, poisoning is an attack, and eviction decides what to drop when the cache is full.

questions.title: With request coalescing on, how many requests reach the origin?
questions.description: At an edge cache, 5,000 requests for the same uncached URL arrive within a few milliseconds.

images.alt: Two panels. Without coalescing, five GET boxes standing in for 5,000 concurrent misses all arrow into one origin box marked 5,000 identical recomputations. With coalescing, the same requests arrow into a single-flight gate labelled one leader, 4,999 waiters, and a single arrow continues to an origin box marked 1 recomputation. Below, four cards name request coalescing, serving stale while revalidating, probabilistic early expiration and TTL jitter, and a final card marks max-age=0 as the opposite of a fix.
images.caption: In the right panel, one leader fetches and 4,999 waiters share the result.

options.text: One, the coalesced (single-flight) fetch; the other 4,999 wait and share its response
5,000, because coalescing only affects retries, not the first wave
Zero, because coalescing serves all 5,000 from the empty cache
2,500, because coalescing halves origin load by batching pairs

questions.explanation: Request coalescing (also called *single-flight* or request collapsing) notices that many concurrent requests want the *same* key. It sends **one** fetch to the origin and gives its response to every waiting request. So 5,000 near-simultaneous misses turn into **one** origin request. It's the most direct defense against stampedes in read-through caches and CDNs. A sudden traffic spike on a cold but cacheable URL doesn't reach the origin at full size. Coalescing can't serve from an empty cache, and it combines the *first* wave of requests, not only retries.

questions.title: What's the difference between `staleTime` and `gcTime` in React Query?
questions.description: In TanStack Query (React Query) v5, `gcTime` is the option that used to be called `cacheTime`.

options.text: `staleTime` is how long data counts as fresh (no background refetch); `gcTime` is how long an *inactive* query's data stays before garbage collection
`staleTime` controls garbage collection; `gcTime` controls how long data is fresh
They are aliases; `gcTime` was simply renamed from `staleTime`
`staleTime` applies to mutations; `gcTime` applies to queries

questions.explanation: They're two separate timers. **`staleTime`** decides how long data stays fresh. While it's fresh, React Query serves it from the cache and skips background refetches. Once it's stale, React Query refetches on triggers like a remount or window refocus. **`gcTime`** decides how long data stays in memory. When nothing on screen uses a query anymore, its data is kept for `gcTime` and then garbage-collected. So a query can be stale and still cached, which lets the library show it instantly and refetch in the background. `gcTime` is the v5 name for `cacheTime`, and `staleTime` kept its name.

questions.title: Why does React Query refetch data it just rendered?
questions.description: A developer notices React Query shows cached data instantly on mount, then immediately fires a network refetch. They haven't set any options.

options.text: The default `staleTime` is `0`, so cached data is stale right away; it's shown immediately, then revalidated
The default `gcTime` is `0`, so the cache is wiped on every mount
React Query never caches `GET` requests without explicit configuration
It's a bug; data should never refetch when it's already in the cache

questions.explanation: React Query's default `staleTime` is **0 ms**, so every query goes stale as soon as it resolves. On remount it shows the cached value right away, with no spinner, then refetches in the background to check for changes. That's intended behavior, and the data really is cached, because `gcTime` defaults to **5 minutes**. For data that changes slowly, raise `staleTime` (for example, `staleTime: 60_000`) to skip the immediate refetch. Mixing up the two timers is the most common React Query mistake.

questions.title: What happens when two components call `useSWR('/api/user')` within about 2 seconds?
questions.description: Vercel's `swr` React hook takes its name from the HTTP `stale-while-revalidate` directive. Both components use the default configuration.

options.text: SWR combines them into a single fetch (the `dedupingInterval`, default 2000 ms), and both components share the result
Each component fires its own independent request; SWR never dedupes
The second call throws, because a key may only be used by one component
Both calls block until a manual `mutate()` is invoked

questions.explanation: SWR groups requests by their key (`'/api/user'`). Within its `dedupingInterval` (default **2000 ms**), identical calls share **one** network request and its result. That's request coalescing on the client. SWR also returns cached data first and then revalidates, which is the HTTP `stale-while-revalidate` idea running in the browser. Components are meant to share keys, and nothing waits for `mutate()`, which you call to update or revalidate the cache yourself.

questions.title: Why does fingerprinting make cache *invalidation* almost a non-problem?
questions.description: Assets ship with content-hashed filenames (`app.7e3a91.js`) and `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable`.

options.text: Each build that changes the file produces a new URL, so you never invalidate the old entry, you just stop linking to it
`immutable` makes the CDN purge old files automatically on each deploy
The one-year `max-age` forces clients to revalidate every request anyway
Content hashes let the browser diff old and new bytes and patch in place

questions.explanation: Fingerprinting avoids the hard problem. The content hash is part of the filename, so *any* change produces a *different URL*. The bytes behind an old URL never change, which makes caching them forever (`max-age=31536000, immutable`) safe. To "invalidate", the HTML points to the new hash, and the old entry does no harm until it's evicted. You don't coordinate a purge or pay for a revalidation round trip. That's why the usual advice is to cache the HTML briefly and its fingerprinted assets forever. Your build tool handles the versioned filenames for you.
